newsitem.title: USA: Higher N.Y. wire fees may cut Canada power imports.
newsitem.headline: Higher N.Y. wire fees may cut Canada power imports.

text.p: Deregulating New York's wholesale electricity market is driving up the cost of sending power on the grid, a factor some industry analysts are warning could cut into imports of cheap electricity from Canada.

The New York Power Authority (NYPA) and Niagara Mohawk Power Corp (NIMO), which together control the main transmission lines across the Canadian border into New York state, have doubled the price they charge all electricity suppliers to move daily, peak, non-firm power on their lines.
"It might have some effect on interruptible energy (sales)," said Marie Archambault, a Hydro-Quebec spokeswoman.
Non-firm, or interruptible power is typically cheaper, purchased by industries on the understanding it can be cut on short notice whenever demand is outpacing supplies.
Hydro-Quebec last year sold 4.9 terawatt hours of non-firm, short-term electricity to utilities in New York state.

Ontario Hydro and Hydro-Quebec, with their vast hydro and nuclear generating capacity, have traditionally provided cheap power to New York, Michigan and New England states to help meet peak air-conditioning demand in the summer.
"It's a little too early to tell (but) we anticipate it could have quite an impact," said Barry Green, market regulation manager at Ontario Hydro.
Market sources said they already see signs of higher transmission costs slowing sales of Canadian power to New York.
"My purchases dropped by half," said a New York utility source, referring to his company's purchase from Hydro-Quebec.
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's (FERC) proposal to deregulate the U.S. electricity industry calls for bulk power prices to be set through competition in an open market.
At the same time, the fees charged for transmitting power over high-voltage lines are to be set by the utilities that own the lines and regulated by a state commission.
These fees, according to FERC's guidelines, must be nondiscriminatory, ensuring equal and open access to anyone seeking to send power across the grid.

But the rules also allow utilities to include in their fees charges needed to recover the money they invested over the years building up their extensive network of lines. And this often means higher transmission costs.
NYPA's new transmission rates took effect this week with their maximum charge for daily, non-firm power jumping to $6.43 per megawatt hour (MWh) from $3.00.
NYPA later retreated, announcing Friday it would return to its previous rate until the mid-March to give the market more time to prepare for the higher rate.
NIMO's highest wheeling rate for daily, non-firm power rose to $6.00/MWh, or about twice what it was charging a month ago, but that it has been granting selective discounts.

"Currently, NIMO is discounting its non-firm rate to $3.00 for all paths except for the Central-East," said a NIMO spokeswoman. The Central-East interface is a gateway for moving power to New York City and New England from western New York.
"We are prepared to come down (in price) depending on the market. We have not been discounting yet. We'll let it ride for a while," NYPA spokesman Ira Fine said.
"We don't have the intention to reduce the price of our product," Archambault said.
Instead, Hydro-Quebec would encourage consumers to pay a higher premium for energy with guaranteed delivery rather than power which could be disrupted, she said.
NYPA's firm transmission capacity of 2,175 megawatts (MW) is fully booked under long-term contracts. It has only an average of 200 MW of non-firm capacity available daily, Fine said.
